To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) many UNESCO World Heritage Sites (UNESCO-WHS) have high cultural diversity; (ii) many UNESCO-WHSs have endangered indigenous languages associated with them; (iii) many UNESCO-WHSSs are located on the same land as endangered languages; and (iv) Australia has the most UNESCO-WHSs with high cultural diversity, many of which have endangered languages associated with them.
Natural World Heritage Sites are often located in areas where indigenous languages are spoken, many of which may be endangered.
the linguistic diversity of natural world heritage sites is an important index of cultural diversity and a key index of conservation opportunity.

the intersection of nature and culture and the need for conservation to bridge this divide.
the intersection of linguistic and natural diversity and the implications for conservation.
the conservation of linguistic and natural diversity and the role of indigenous peoples in this endeavour.

there is a need for a more integrated and holistic approach to conservation of both cultural and natural heritage.
linguistic diversity is an important part of the natural world, and that natural world heritage sites are a key component of cultural heritage.
the co-occurrences of Natural WHS and linguistic diversity are not only important for the preservation of biodiversity, but also for the protection of cultural heritage.

there is a strong correlation between linguistic diversity and Natural WHSs.
the world's most important natural places are often also home to the most linguistically diverse places on the planet.
